name: The Khamsa
powers: Deflects the evil eye and brings blessing to its bearer.
description: The open-hand amulet of the Maghreb and wider Middle East, called the Hand of Fatima after the Prophet's daughter and the Hand of Miriam in Jewish usage, hung in homes, worn as jewelry, and painted on doorways against the evil eye. The silver khamsa was the standard talisman of North African Jews and Muslims alike, with pieces from sheet silver to fine filigree set with coral.

name: The Gris-gris
maker: Fqih (learned man) who wrote the contents
powers: Protects, heals, or brings luck by the written words sealed inside.
description: A small leather pouch worn on the body, holding written Qur'anic verses, prayers, or magic squares, used across North Africa to protect, heal, or bring fortune. In Morocco the hirz was stitched by a fqih and worn at the neck or arm, its power resting entirely on the writing sealed inside. The custom is documented in ethnographic surveys of Maghrebi folk practice and survives today.
source: Ethnographic surveys of Maghrebi folk practice

name: The Tunisian Fibula
powers: Fastened the shawl and served as a bridal heirloom and protective talisman.
description: The large silver pin or brooch, often triangular with a central coral or enamel stud and a long pointed pin, worn by Amazigh women across Tunisia, Algeria, and Morocco to fasten the shawl and passed down as a bridal heirloom. Its form echoes Roman-era brooches of the region, and its silver and coral decoration is documented in museum collections of Maghrebi dress.

name: Tagine Cooking Vessel
description: The tagine is the conical clay cooking vessel of Morocco, whose tall lid traps steam so that slow-braised stews cook in very little water. The same word names the dish it cooks; the pot is glazed, set over a brazier or stove, and has become emblematic of Moroccan cooking and hospitality across North Africa.

name: Burnous Cloak
description: The burnous is the hooded, sleeveless woollen cloak of the Berbers of North Africa, woven in one piece with a pointed hood (qob). Worn by men over other garments, it shields against sun and cold and marks status; finely embroidered burnouses are reserved for ceremonies and celebrations.

name: Tizerzai Brooch
powers: Fastens the dress and is worn for protection, with engraved motifs said to avert harm.
description: The tizerzai is a large silver brooch of the Amazigh women of Morocco, a crescent- or triangle-shaped clasp used to fasten the shoulder of the dress, fitted with a long pin and decorative chainwork. It is both a practical garment fastener and a piece of protective jewellery, often engraved and embellished with coral or enamel.

name: Kabyle Earthenware
description: Kabyle earthenware of Algeria is burnished, hand-built clay pottery made by Kabyle women in the Djurdjura mountains, shaped without a wheel and decorated with painted or incised geometric motifs. Cooking pots, water jars, and grain bowls served daily life; the reddish clay pieces are famed for their clean lines and remain a living craft of the Berber home.

name: Chaoui Aures Kilim
description: Chaoui (Aures) weavings of Algeria are wool carpets and blankets woven on ground looms by Amazigh women of the Aures mountains, with bold stripes and geometric medallions in red, brown, and cream. Woven for the home and for dowries, the textiles carry regional motifs whose meanings are handed down in the weaving tradition.
source: Studies of Amazigh weaving (e.g. Ianthe Reswick)

name: Tunisian Chechia Cap
description: The chechia is the brimless, red felt cap of Tunisia, traditionally made by hand-felting wool and dyeing it crimson, then shaping it over a wooden mould. Worn by men across the Maghreb as a mark of Tunisian identity, it was produced in the chechia craft quarter of Tunis and given as a gift of distinction.

name: Gourgui Water Jar
description: The gourgui is a porous clay water jar of Tunisia, kept in the cool shade of the home so that evaporation chills the water inside. Its narrow neck and globular body recall ancient amphorae; similar jars across the Maghreb were central to daily water storage and hospitality.

name: Garamantian Rock-Art Chariot
description: Rock-art depictions of horses and chariots carved in the Tadrart Acacus and Messak mountains of the Fezzan, Libya, are linked in scholarship to the Garamantes, the Saharan power whose chariot-based trade crossed the desert. The engravings, several thousand years old, show lightweight chariots in motion and form a major record of Saharan history.
source: UNESCO rock-art sites of Tadrart Acacus; Garamantian archaeology

name: Canopic Jar
era: Ancient Egyptian (Old Kingdom to Ptolemaic era)
description: Canopic jars are the lidded stone or pottery vessels of ancient Egypt that held the embalmed organs of the dead, each guarded by one of the Four Sons of Horus. Made from the Old Kingdom onward, they were buried with the mummy so the body would be whole in the afterlife; Anubis, god of mummification, presides over the rite.
source: Ancient Egyptian funerary archaeology; museum collections

name: Ancient Egyptian Kohl Tube
description: Ancient Egyptian kohl tubes are slender cosmetic containers, often of wood, stone, or faience, used to hold kohl eye-paint. Applied with a stick, kohl protected the eyes from sun and flies and carried religious meaning, its dark-lined eye echoing the apotropaic gaze of Horus; fine decorated examples survive from the New Kingdom.
source: Museum collections (British Museum, Metropolitan Museum of Art)

name: Sudanese Kaskara Sword
description: The kaskara is a straight, double-edged sword with a plain iron cross-guard and disc pommel, carried in Sudan and adjacent regions into the 20th century. It descends from medieval Arab forms and served as a fighting blade and ceremonial weapon; many bear inscriptions, marks, or leather-wrapped grips, and were worn as signs of honour.

name: Sudanese Girba Water-Skin
description: The girba is a water vessel of Sudan made from a whole tanned animal hide, treated to be watertight, with openings at the neck and legs. Carried by travellers and herders across the Sahel and Nubia, it keeps water cool through evaporation; its shape and use are documented in travel accounts of the Nile lands.
source: Travel accounts of the Nile lands; museum collections
